claims_guardrails: No source, no verdict: every figure traces to sources/.

Counts are REAL: 315 questions = 219 topic (node) + 96 connection (one per hard edge). Validated: every concept + hard edge covered; every question 4 options; every answer_key matches an option. Difficulty 1-3.

Real examples: node 'most abundant molecule, 70%+ of mass?' -> Water (opts Water/Protein/DNA/Lipid); connection 'how do mutations support oncogene activation?' -> 'caused by specific mutation types, so you need mutations first'.

The demo (student_roadmap_app.html): pick goal -> build roadmap (each step linked to chapter/section + reason) -> quick check (pass skips topic + what it builds on; miss keeps it) -> roadmap from where you are (done/start here/upcoming). Offline, real book.

HONEST BOUNDARY: every question a DRAFT (approve blank; llm_proposed; needs_review=yes). Empty-body-text sections anchored to section title + standard textbook facts. Complete + validated but NOT verified -> needs faculty. No learning-outcome claim.

beats.narration_text: Hello, fellows. Last week the gate ran, but on placeholder questions. The real next step was clear: write an actual question for every part of the roadmap, and get faculty to check them. So this week — the full question bank, three hundred fifteen of them, plus a working demo of what a student actually sees. The question: how do you make a whole curriculum's questions something a faculty reviewer can actually verify?

beats.narration_text: Three moves make a question bank verifiable. One: cover everything — one question for every topic, and one for every hard prerequisite link. No gaps. Two: every question carries its receipts — four options, the right answer, a one-line reason, a difficulty, and the exact chapter and section it came from. Three: ship it as a draft — an empty approve column on every row, nothing trusted until a faculty member signs it off. Cover it, back it with sources, leave it open for review.

beats.narration_text: Here's one question, in full. From chapter one, normal cell biology: which molecule is most abundant in cells, seventy percent or more of total mass? Four options — water, protein, DNA, lipid. The answer: water, with a one-line reason tied back to the section. A difficulty, one to three. And the exact section it's drawn from. Everything a reviewer needs to say yes, or fix it, in a single row.

beats.narration_text: Two kinds of question. A topic question asks do you know this. A connection question asks something harder: do you see how one topic supports the next? For example — how do mutations support understanding how oncogenes get activated? The answer: oncogene activation is caused by specific mutation types, so you need mutations first. That's the question that tests the link, not just the facts — grounded in the prerequisite's own reason.

beats.narration_text: And to see it all work together, a demo of the student experience — running in a browser, driven by the real book. A student picks what they want to learn. The tool builds the full roadmap to that goal, in order, each step linked to its exact chapter and section, with a reason it's needed. It offers a quick check from the real questions — pass a topic and it's skipped, along with what it builds on; miss one and it stays in the plan. Then it shows the path from where the student actually is: done, start here, and what's coming.

beats.narration_text: What's honest about it. Every question is a draft — the approve column is blank, nothing is confirmed. And a few sections came through with empty body text, so those questions are anchored to the section title and standard textbook facts, not the exact wording — which is exactly what the review will catch. The bank is complete and validated; it is not yet verified. That's the next step, and it needs faculty.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you're building a question bank for review: cover every node and every link; make every question carry its answer, its reason, and its exact source; and leave an approve column for the expert. A complete, sourced draft is what makes a review fast — and a review is what makes it real.
